body:
## Problem

TraitMech contains a correctness fix in scripts/_edison_capture.py that records which sidecars the current invocation actually wrote.

CultureMech, MediaIngredientMech, and CommunityMech still determine sidecar presence from files already on disk. Edison output stems are deterministic. On a rerun, a prior response, agent-state, or files sidecar can remain present even when the new invocation did not fetch it, causing the new metadata record to attribute stale provenance to a different task_id.

This is an auditability defect in shared paid-research capture code.

## Proposed scope

1. Treat the TraitMech current-invocation written-set behavior as the candidate canonical fix.
2. Add a regression test with pre-existing sidecars and a new response that does not rewrite all of them.
3. Propagate the fixed capture module and tests to CultureMech, MediaIngredientMech, and CommunityMech.
4. Put _edison_capture.py under shared drift enforcement or move it to a shared package.
5. Confirm enrich_edison_response and dry-run behavior remain correct.

## Acceptance criteria

- Metadata reports true only for sidecars produced by the current invocation.
- A stale sidecar from a previous run is never attributed to the new task_id.
- All four Edison-capable Mechs run the same regression test.
- Shared capture code is protected from future unreviewed drift.
- Tests use fixtures or mocks and spend no provider credits.

Fleet review: CultureBotAI/culturebotai-claw docs/reviews/five_mech_shared_functionality_review.md
title: Propagate current-run Edison sidecar provenance tracking across Mechs

body:
## Problem

scripts/deep_research_provider.py and tests/test_deep_research_provider.py are currently byte-identical across CultureMech, TraitMech, MediaIngredientMech, CommunityMech, and ProteinTraitsMech.

They are copied into every repository but are not included in the vendored-sync contract. A provider-status, scoring, policy, or JSON-output fix can therefore land in one Mech while the other four remain silently stale.

The previous fleet review also found shared routing defects that need one implementation point: query classification is manual, stage recommendations are advisory rather than executable, provider health checks are shallow, cost policy is not enforceable, and provider-filtered JSON can retain recommendations for another provider.

## Proposed scope

Choose one supported sharing model:

1. Move the generic provider catalog, status checks, scoring, report model, and CLI into culturebotai-claw and keep only domain profiles in each Mech; or
2. Keep vendored scripts but add the implementation and tests to the canonical pinned vendored-sync contract.

Domain-specific YAML profiles should remain local.

## Acceptance criteria

- There is one authoritative implementation and test suite.
- Every Mech consumes or verifies that implementation automatically.
- Shared fixes cannot merge in one repository while the fleet silently diverges.
- The implementation supports policy constraints such as provider allowlists and no-paid-provider mode.
- Machine-readable output is internally consistent when filtered to one provider.
- No provider call is required by drift or unit tests.

Related: #284 covers the deep-research-client version upgrade; this issue covers fleet ownership and drift after the upgrade.
title: Protect shared deep-research provider triage from fleet drift

body:
Found by the new Codex research path on its **first real run** (#284), then verified
independently against the MediaDive API.

`data/normalized_yaml/bacterial/lb_broth.yaml` carries:

```yaml
kg_microbe_match: mediadive.medium:74
```

MediaDive 74 is **THERMUS THERMOPHILUS MEDIUM**. LB is MediaDive **381**
(`LB (Luria-Bertani) MEDIUM`). Both confirmed by fetching them.

## It is not one record

494 records carry a `mediadive.medium:` typed `kg_microbe_match`, and the values cluster
implausibly:

| medium | records pointing at it | what it actually is |
|---|---:|---|
| `mediadive.medium:12` | 119 | SOIL EXTRACT MEDIUM |
| `mediadive.medium:101` | 81 | NUTRIENT AGAR or BROTH WITH NaCl |
| `mediadive.medium:74` | **75** | THERMUS THERMOPHILUS MEDIUM |

Name-checking the first 8 with the same `names_agree` guard used for the KOMODO
resolution (#239/#244):

```
MISMATCH chm      -> C78  PM
MISMATCH eg       -> C78  PM
MISMATCH lb       ->  74  THERMUS THERMOPHILUS MEDIUM
MISMATCH my75s    ->  12  SOIL EXTRACT MEDIUM
OK       pm       -> C78  PM
MISMATCH sna      -> 101  NUTRIENT AGAR or BROTH WITH NaCl
MISMATCH sna_5    -> 101  NUTRIENT AGAR or BROTH WITH NaCl
MISMATCH ypd_agar ->  12  SOIL EXTRACT MEDIUM
```

**7 of 8.** Some are unambiguous — `lb` is not Thermus medium, `ypd_agar` is not soil
extract.

A caveat I would want tested before acting: `names_agree` is a heuristic and produced
false positives elsewhere, so a fraction of these may be legitimate matches under a
different name. But 75 records sharing one id, and that id being a named-organism medium,
is not explicable that way.

## Why it matters

The field name says it is the join into KG-Microbe. If it is wrong at this rate, anything
consuming it is associating media with unrelated organisms — and unlike the grounding
defects fixed recently, this one has had no detector at all.

## Suggested

1. Name-check all 494 against MediaDive and report, reusing `names_agree` and the
   composition comparison built for #262 — composition is the stronger test and settled
   the KOMODO cases where names had diverged.
2. Decide per cluster: the three big ids look like a default or fallback that was written
   in rather than resolved.
3. Add a standing gate, as with #278's element check, so this cannot silently regrow.

Worth noting how this surfaced: nobody looked for it. A research run on an unrelated
question (`what organisms grow in LB?`) read the record and said the mapping was wrong.
title: kg_microbe_match points at the wrong MediaDive medium in most records sampled (7 of 8)

body:
We do use it — as a **CLI subprocess**, not a Python import. `scripts/research_media.py`
shells out to `deep-research-client` (`--client-command`, default `deep-research-client`),
and it is declared in the `dev` extra as `deep-research-client[cyberian]>=0.2.4`. Nothing
imports `deep_research_client` in Python. It resolves from **PyPI**, not from the DisMech
repo.

It is installed and the CLI works. The problem is that it is stale, and staleness has
cost us work.

## Version state

| | version | providers available |
|---|---|---|
| CultureMech (installed) | **0.2.4** | `cyberian` only — verified with `deep-research-client providers` |
| PyPI latest | **0.2.10** | OpenAI, **Edison**, Asta, Perplexity, Consensus, Cyberian, OpenScientist, **Claude Code (local CLI)** |
| DisMech | **0.1.3**, declared unpinned | older still |

## Two consequences

**1. The documented reason for bypassing it is obsolete.** `scripts/research_media_edison.py`
says:

> Uses the `edison-client` SDK directly. The companion `research_media.py` wraps
> `deep-research-client`, but **as of DRC 0.2.4 only `cyberian` and `openai` are registered
> providers — Edison/PaperQA is not exposed there**, so we drive the SDK directly.

0.2.10 exposes Edison (`falcon`/`edison`/`eds`/`science`, "powered by PaperQA3"). So the
whole second code path exists to work around a limitation that has since been lifted, and
we now maintain two research entry points instead of one.

**2. We reimplemented a provider the library already has.** When Edison started returning
HTTP 402 earlier, the fallback was a hand-rolled native-Claude research path in
`.claude/skills/deep-research-medium/SKILL.md`. 0.2.10 ships **Claude Code (local CLI)** as
a first-class provider behind the same interface. That fallback could have been a
`--provider` flag.

## Also worth checking on upgrade

Our `.env.example` sets `EDISON_PLATFORM_API_KEY` (with a note that the SDK reads it
natively), but DRC's own table expects **`EDISON_API_KEY`**. If the Edison provider is
adopted through DRC rather than the SDK, that name has to be reconciled or the provider
will silently not auto-detect — DRC "auto-detects providers from environment variables",
so a wrong name presents as "provider unavailable", not as an error.

## Suggested

1. Bump to `>=0.2.10`, re-run `deep-research-client providers`, and record what actually
   registers — the `[cyberian]` extra may need widening for the others.
2. If Edison registers, retire `research_media_edison.py`'s SDK bypass and its docstring
   rationale, collapsing to one entry point.
3. Evaluate the Claude Code provider against the hand-rolled skill path; keep whichever is
   better, but not both by accident.
4. Coordinate with DisMech, which is on 0.1.3 and unpinned — an unpinned shared dependency
   across repos is how the two drift apart silently.

Not urgent in the sense that nothing is broken today; the research lane is dormant. Urgent
in the sense that it is the lane we reach for when the corpus needs evidence (#150's 185
cocktails, #279, #273 all need source reading), and it should not be discovered stale at
the moment of need.
title: deep-research-client is 6 releases stale (0.2.4 vs 0.2.10); the reason we bypass it no longer holds

body:
Found probing #282 for rename-induced collisions. It is **not** caused by that PR — the
same rows exist on main under the corrupted spellings — but repairing the names made it
legible.

`data/normalized_yaml/algae/ucm.yaml` (and its merged twin) carries each of two trace
elements **twice**, at values exactly 1000× apart:

| ingredient | value A | value B | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| `As2O3` (was `As O`) | 0.000093 g/L | 0.093 g/L | 1000× |
| `Na2WO4.2H2O` (was `Na WO .2H O`) | 0.000066 g/L | 0.066 g/L | 1000× |

Both rows in each pair carry the same grounding and the same source
(`CCAP Medium MR_UCM.pdf`).

A factor of exactly 1000 between two copies of one ingredient is the **flattened-cocktail
signature** from #150: the stock-strength value and the final per-litre value both present
as sibling ingredient rows, rather than the stock nested under a `solutions:` entry with an
addition volume. Here it has not been flattened *into* the medium — both readings are
sitting next to each other, which is arguably worse, because any consumer summing
ingredients counts the trace element at ~1000× its real contribution.

Worth checking against the CCAP source PDF which figure is the medium's and which is the
stock's, then either nesting the stock (the #150 repair) or dropping the stock-strength
row.

Also worth a corpus-wide sweep for the same shape — two rows, one name, values differing
by a clean factor of 1000 — since this one only surfaced by accident. The existing
`audit_concentration_plausibility` looks at absolute magnitude, not at ratios between
sibling rows, so it would not catch this pattern.

Related: #263 removed rows duplicated *verbatim*; this is the sibling case where the
duplicate carries a different value and so is a real (wrong) datum rather than redundancy.
title: ucm.yaml lists the same trace elements twice, 1000x apart — stock strength and final concentration side by side

body:
Salvaged from `feat/id-label-correspondence` (PR #44, closed unmerged, 2026-06-10) while
clearing stale branches. Main's validator has since grown to 988 lines against that
branch's 614, so the branch is superseded — **except for one thing main never picked up.**

`scripts/validate_id_label_correspondence.py` is vendored **byte-identical across the Mech
repos**. The branch pinned it:

```
scripts/.validate_id_label_correspondence.sha256
0a446a80ae932f229a45d69995f1e68a1409ef0bb89479a77d5f08265ee0c582  scripts/validate_id_label_correspondence.py
```

with two justfile targets — `verify-validator-pin` (run in CI, `sha256sum -c`, falling back
to `shasum -a 256` on macOS) and `refresh-validator-pin` for a deliberate all-repos update.

Main has the validator and the `label-correspondence` workflow, but **no pin**. So a local
edit to one repo's copy diverges silently, and the copies drift apart with nothing
reporting it. That is the specific risk the pin existed for.

To be precise about scope, since I first described this more broadly than it is: the pin
guards **cross-repo vendoring drift**, not a validator that stops detecting. Those are
different problems. It does not verify the script still works — only that it is the same
bytes everywhere.

Both are worth having, and the second is the one this repo has actually been bitten by
(#277's absent CI gates, #272's classifier reporting zero splits, #275's `yaml.dump`
no-op). The pin is cheap and independently useful; a "does the detector still detect"
guard is the harder and more valuable sibling, and every audit script added since #266
now carries an anti-vacuous test toward that end.

Suggested: restore the pin file and the two targets, add `verify-validator-pin` to the
`label-correspondence` workflow, and re-pin against main's current 988-line version rather
than the stale hash above — the hash is recorded here only so the branch can be deleted
without losing it.

The hash above corresponds to the branch's 614-line version and is **not** valid for main.
title: Recover the sha256 pin for the vendored id-label validator before feat/id-label-correspondence is deleted

body:
Found by the element-mismatch detector added for #276/#278.

Three groundings replace selenium or silicon with **sulfur** — the same substitution three
times, which makes it a systematic cause rather than three typos:

| ingredient | grounded to | which is | should be |
|---|---|---|---|
| `H2SeO3` | CHEBI:48854 | **sulfurous** acid | selenous acid (CHEBI:26642) |
| `Na2SeO4 x 10 H2O` | CHEBI:32586 | sodium **sulfate** decahydrate | sodium selenate decahydrate |
| `Na2SiO3 x 5 H2O` | CHEBI:86477 | sodium **sulfite** | sodium metasilicate pentahydrate |

The `H2SeO3` case is fixed (2 rows). **The other two cannot be**: ChEBI has no term for
`sodium selenate decahydrate` or `sodium metasilicate pentahydrate`. Regrounding them to a
near-miss would repeat the error in a new place.

They are recorded in `tests/test_name_term_elements.py` as `KNOWN_WRONG_PENDING_279`,
deliberately separate from the `KNOWN_NO_SALT_TERM` allowlist above it. That distinction
matters: one set is "ChEBI lacks the salt, the free acid is the best available answer", the
other is "this is wrong and we have not fixed it". A test asserts the wrong-set stays at
exactly 2, so it cannot quietly absorb new defects.

Options:
1. **Unground them** — set no `term`, as was done for `Infusion from Potatoes` in #266.
   Honestly unmapped beats confidently wrong, and this is what I would do absent a better
   target.
2. **Ground to the parent** — `selenate` / `silicate` without the hydrate and cation. Less
   wrong, still imprecise.
3. **Request the terms from ChEBI.** Correct in the long run and slow.

Worth chasing the shared cause too. Three independent Se/Si → S substitutions suggests
something upstream — a fuzzy name match scoring `selenate`/`silicate` against `sulfate`, or
a lookup keyed on a normalized string where the distinguishing letters were already lost
(compare the subscript-stripping in #276, where `Na WO .2H O` lost its digits). Whatever
produced these probably produced others that happen to land on a plausible compound and so
are invisible to this detector.
title: Selenate read as sulfate, silicate as sulfite: Se/Si groundings collapsing onto their sulfur analogues

body:
Found reviewing #275, and caused by it.

Until now, a wrong grounding was visible because `term.label` held the ingredient string
while the id pointed somewhere else — `Na2-EDTA x 2 H2O` sitting next to a term that is
actually *EDTA disodium salt (anhydrous)*. That mismatch is what surfaced the 413 rows
#275 corrected, and before that it is what made #256/#257 findable at all.

#275 sets every label from the ontology. **Every label now agrees with its id, including
any id that is wrong.** The detector was accidental, and it is now gone: after this PR a
mis-grounded row looks exactly like a correct one.

That is still the right change — a label field should hold the label — but it leaves a
hole that should be filled deliberately rather than by accident.

## The replacement

Compare the ingredient's **`preferred_term`** against its grounded term's label, and flag
where they contradict on something checkable. Hydration is the tractable case and was
worth 413 rows in #275 alone:

```
preferred_term: Na2-EDTA x 2 H2O   →  2 waters
term.label:     EDTA disodium salt (anhydrous)  →  0 waters
                                       ^ contradiction
```

The parsing already exists in `audit_grounding_consistency.py` (the `HYDRATE` regex and
its water-count logic) and in the one-off scan used for #275. It needs lifting into a
standing check.

Scope, in order of confidence:

1. **Hydration mismatch** — name says N waters, term says M. Unambiguous. Currently 18
   known survivors (`FeSO4 x 6 H2O` / `x 5 H2O`, `VOSO4 x 5 H2O`) which CHEBI has no term
   for, so the check needs an allowlist or they will be permanent noise.
2. **Salt vs ion** — name says `KNO3`, term label says `nitrate`. Detectable via the
   ION heuristic already in the audit script.
3. **Element mismatch** — name contains `Mg`, term label says `potassium aluminium`.
   Cheap and would have caught the CHEBI:86463 case in #257 directly.

(3) is the one I would add first — it is the crudest and it catches the worst class, the
one where the grounded term is a completely different substance.

Run it as a CI gate with a baseline count, like the other anti-vacuous gates in this repo,
so it cannot silently pass when the detector breaks (see #277 and the classifier bug in
#272 — both were failures that looked like success).
title: #275 removes the accidental detector for wrong groundings; replace it with a real one

body:
Found on #275. **Four of the six gates did not run, and nothing said so.** The PR shows two
green checks and looks fully verified.

## What happened

GitHub evaluates `on.pull_request.paths` filters against only the **first 300 changed
files** of a PR. #275 changes **20,634** files, and of the first 300, **zero** are under
`data/normalized_yaml/` — they are all `data/merge_yaml/merged/`, which sorts first.

So every workflow filtered solely on `data/normalized_yaml/**` failed to match and never
ran:

| workflow | filters on `merge_yaml`? | ran on #275? |
|---|---|---|
| `label-correspondence` | **yes** | ✅ |
| `tests` (pytest) | no path filter | ✅ |
| `chebi-consistency` | no (only in a comment) | ❌ |
| `concentration-plausibility` | no | ❌ |
| `curation-history` | no | ❌ |
| `validate` | no | ❌ |

`label-correspondence` ran *only* because it happens to also list `data/merge_yaml/**`.

## Why this is worse than a flaky gate

A skipped check is **not** reported as skipped — it is simply absent from `gh pr checks`,
and the PR reads as green. The failure mode is exactly the one this repo keeps hitting: an
output indistinguishable from success. I nearly merged #275 on two green checks.

It also scales the wrong way. The bigger and more sweeping the change — precisely when the
gates matter most — the more likely the first 300 files miss the filter.

## Mitigations, roughly in order

1. **Add `data/merge_yaml/**` to every workflow that filters on `data/normalized_yaml/**`.**
   Cheapest fix, and correct on its own terms: `chebi-consistency`'s own comment already
   says merge_yaml is unguarded and asks for this if it is ever hand-edited. #266 and #275
   both edited it directly, so that condition is now met.
2. **Drop the path filters on the data gates entirely.** They exist to save CI minutes on
   docs-only PRs; the gates are cheap (2–4 min) relative to the risk.
3. **A required "all gates reported" check** that fails when an expected workflow is absent,
   so silence is loud.

(1) plus (3) is what I would do — (1) fixes the immediate hole, (3) stops the next variant
of it.

## For #275 specifically

I ran the four skipped gates locally: `just check-chebi-grounding` exit 0,
`just audit-concentration-plausibility` exit 0, `just validate-strict` 0 errors over
15,877 files. `curation-history` is advisory only and does not block. So that PR is
verified — but by hand, not by CI.
title: Large PRs silently skip most CI gates: path filters see only the first 300 changed files

body:
Found while working the #260 direction from the MIM side. MediaIngredientMech needs records for the 44 CultureMech ingredient names it lacks, so I verified CultureMech's `term.id` for each before adopting it. **They should not be adopted as-is.**

## 1. One grounding names an unrelated compound

    Sodium sulfide  ->  CHEBI:85357

`CHEBI:85357` is **`3-[(1E,4R)-4-hydroxycyclohex-2-en-1-ylidene]pyruvic acid`**, formula `C9H10O4` — an organic acid. Sodium sulfide is `Na2S`:

    CHEBI:76208  sodium sulfide (anhydrous)   2Na.S
    CHEBI:76209  sodium sulfide nonahydrate   9H2O.2Na.S

This is the same shape as the `Cysteine-HCl` → `CHEBI:52891` (a fluorescent quencher dye) error I flagged on #272. Two independent instances suggests a systematic cause rather than two typos — worth finding whatever produced both.

**The cheap detector**: compare the ChEBI *label* of each assigned id against the ingredient name and flag any pair sharing no token. It is how `KF` → `Lys-Phe` was caught in MIM.

## 2. Stereochemistry silently dropped

    DL-Tyrosine    ->  CHEBI:17895  L-tyrosine
    DL-threonine   ->  CHEBI:16857  L-threonine

A racemate is not its L-enantiomer. `CHEBI:18186 tyrosine` is stereo-unspecified and closer; ChEBI has no `DL-threonine` term, so that one may need a registry mint rather than a wrong answer.

## 3. Labels have lost their subscripts

Eight ingredient names are unreadable as chemistry because the digits are gone:

| stored label | almost certainly |
|---|---|
| `H BO` | H₃BO₃ boric acid |
| `ZnCl .6H O` | ZnCl₂·6H₂O |
| `Co(NO ) .6H O` | Co(NO₃)₂·6H₂O |
| `LiCl.H O` | LiCl·H₂O |
| `As O` | As₂O₃ |
| `Na WO .2H O` | Na₂WO₄·2H₂O |
| `TeO` | TeO₂ |
| `MgSO .7H2O` | MgSO₄·7H₂O |

Note `MgSO .7H2O` keeps the `2` in `H2O` but loses the `4` — so this is not a uniform strip. It looks like subscript characters (₂₃₄) were dropped while ASCII digits survived, which points at an encoding step rather than a parser.

Related typos in the same set, possibly the same origin: `MgSO2·7H2O` (should be SO₄), `NaMoO4·2H2O` ×4 spellings (should be Na₂MoO₄), `Na2Se3 x 5 H2O`, `Na2SeO·5H2O`, `NaSeO3·5H2O`, `Ferric ammmonium citrate`, `Distiled water`.

## Why this matters for #260

Under the agreed direction MIM is the source of truth, so these names need MIM records. But **MIM must not inherit these groundings** — importing them would move the defects rather than fix them, and MIM has no way to tell a good CultureMech id from a bad one without checking each.

So the 44 split roughly:

* ~8 subscript-stripped labels — should be **repaired here**, not recreated in MIM
* ~10 typos and notation variants — likewise
* ~13 genuinely new ingredients MIM should hold, but grounded independently
* the rest are notation variants of substances MIM already has, which become synonyms rather than records

Repairing (1)–(3) here is the higher-value half, because it fixes the source rather than propagating it.
title: Ingredient groundings include a wrong compound, dropped stereochemistry, and subscript-stripped labels

body:
Noticed while canarying #263's dedup.

`data/normalized_yaml/algae/sbbm.yaml` carried this as an ingredient row:

```yaml
- preferred_term: Make up to 1 litre with distilled water. For agar add
  concentration:
    value: '15'
    unit: G_PER_L
  source: CCAP Medium MR_SBBM.pdf
```

That is a preparation instruction from the source PDF, parsed as an ingredient and given
the concentration of whatever followed it (the 15 g/l is presumably the agar). It appeared
twice, which is how the dedup pass surfaced it.

Two distinct harms:

1. **A phantom ingredient.** Anything counting ingredients, exporting to KG-Microbe, or
   computing composition sees a component that does not exist.
2. **A misattributed concentration.** If the 15 g/l belongs to agar, then agar is either
   missing its concentration or carrying a different one — worth checking which.

This is likely not one record. Candidate detection: `preferred_term` containing a verb
phrase, sentence punctuation, or exceeding some length — real ingredient names are short
noun phrases. A quick scan for `preferred_term` values containing `. ` or more than ~6
words would size it.

Related: #265 (ingredient synonyms effectively unpopulated) and #259 (`term.label` carrying
ingredient strings) are both symptoms of the same underlying thing — the ingredient field
is absorbing text it was not meant to hold.
title: Preparation instructions are parsed as ingredients with concentrations

body:
Found reviewing #270, and it is a two-sided finding — both repos have the same defect,
so a fix on either side alone leaves the split in place.

`L-cysteine hydrochloride monohydrate` is written several ways across the corpus. MIM's
`UNIFIED_INGREDIENT_MAPPING.tsv` grounds those spellings to **two different terms**, split
by nothing but punctuation:

| ingredient name | MIM `mim_id` | is |
|---|---|---|
| `L-Cysteine HCl x H2O` (space) | CHEBI:91248 | L-cysteine hydrochloride hydrate ✅ |
| `L-Cysteine・HCl・H2O` | CHEBI:91248 | ✅ |
| `L-cysteine HCl.H2O` | CHEBI:91248 | ✅ |
| `L-Cysteine hydrochloride monohydrate` | CHEBI:91248 | ✅ |
| **`L-Cysteine-HCl x H2O`** (hyphen) | **CHEBI:17561** | plain L-cysteine ❌ |
| **`Cysteine-HCl x H2O`** | **CHEBI:17561** | ❌ |
| **`Cysteine-HCl·H2O`** | **CHEBI:17561** | ❌ |
| **`L-cysteine-HCL x H2O`** | **CHEBI:17561** | ❌ |

Same substance, same source, and the only difference is whether `HCl` is preceded by a
space or a hyphen. CHEBI:17561 is neither the salt nor the hydrate.

CultureMech had exactly the same split — #270 fixes our side, moving the hyphenated forms
to CHEBI:91248 to match what both repos already do for the spaced forms (1,901 rows here,
and MIM's own mapping above).

**Consequence for the divergence count.** After #270, 63 ingredient rows have
`culturemech_term_id` = CHEBI:91248 against MIM's `mim_id` = CHEBI:17561. Per
MediaIngredientMech#138's precedence chain, ours wins downstream — so kg-microbe gets the
right answer. But the divergence is real and will show up in any future join, and MIM's
copy stays wrong for anyone reading MIM directly.

Worth reporting upstream so MIM's hyphenated variants move to CHEBI:91248 too. That is a
MIM-side edit; I have not filed it there.

Related: #258 (one ingredient name, several CHEBI ids) is the same disease in a different
compound family — the general fix is a normalization step that collapses punctuation
before grounding, rather than curating each spelling.
title: MIM and CultureMech both split L-cysteine HCl monohydrate by punctuation: 'x H2O' vs '-HCl x H2O'

body:
Found reviewing #268, which promotes a KOMODO volume to an assertion when the record
reproduces the fetched medium's composition exactly over `MIN_SHARED_COMPOUNDS` (8) or
more compounds.

The threshold counts **all** shared compounds. But a medium's identity lives in its main
solution: two different media that both add SL-10 and Seven vitamins share ~14 stock
compounds at identical values for free, because a stock's composition is the same
wherever it is used. Only the main-solution salts distinguish one medium from another.

Measured across the 23 records #268 promoted:

| shared compounds from the MAIN solution | records |
|---:|---:|
| 4 | 1 (`sypc_medium.yaml`, medium 1188) |
| 5–7 | 7 |
| 8–13 | 15 |

So the premise holds in practice — every promotion had main-solution agreement, and the
unrelated-media control scored 0.00 — but nothing in the code *requires* it. A future
record that shares only its stocks with the fetched medium would pass on 8 stock
compounds alone and get a volume asserted on no distinguishing evidence at all.

Proposed: split the threshold.

```python
MIN_SHARED_COMPOUNDS = 8        # total, as now
MIN_MAIN_SOLUTION_COMPOUNDS = 4 # NEW: excluding compounds that come from a referenced stock
```

`extract_additions` already identifies which solutions are cocktail stocks (the
`COCKTAIL_NAME` regex in `fetch_mediadive_solution_volumes.py`), so the main-solution set
is available without new fetching.

Worth re-checking `sypc_medium.yaml` by hand while doing this — at 4 main-solution
compounds it is the thinnest evidence in the promoted set, and if the rule lands at 5 it
would need to be demoted back to a candidate.
title: Composition-match promotion should require a minimum of MAIN-solution compounds, not just total shared

body:
Found while addressing #260. This is a process gap, not a one-off.

`data/merge_yaml/merged` is a **derived product** of `data/normalized_yaml` (justfile:
"Merging duplicate recipes from normalized_yaml to merge_yaml"), but it is tracked in git
(6,326 files) and is not regenerated by `just refresh-derived`. So a script that fixes the
corpus silently fixes only half of it.

Concretely: PR #257 corrected wrong-compound groundings and ran only against
`normalized_yaml`. **After #257 merged**, the merged corpus still carried:

| id | actually is | merged files still wrong |
|---|---|---:|
| `CHEBI:42758` | aldehydo-D-glucose (open-chain tautomer) | 608 |
| `CHEBI:86463` | potassium aluminium sulfate, on `Magnesium Sulfate Heptahydrate` | 118 rows |

#266 cleaned both up (1,359 rows / 717 merged records) while doing #260, and afterwards
**0 of 1,571** ingredient names shared by the two corpora have a disagreeing modal
grounding. But nothing prevents the next fix from re-opening the gap.

The failure mode is quiet: `validate-strict` passes, tests pass, the fix looks complete,
and the stale half keeps publishing the wrong id downstream. It is the same shape as the
derived-artifact drift class in #145, one level up.

Options, roughly in order of preference:

1. **Regenerate `merge_yaml` as part of `just refresh-derived`** and let the drift check
   fail when it is stale. Correct in principle — it is a build product — but the merge
   step needs to be deterministic enough that regenerating does not produce a large
   unrelated diff. Worth measuring before committing to it.
2. **Have corpus-fix scripts default to both roots.** Cheap; `fix_wrong_compound_groundings.py`
   already takes `--yaml-dir`, so this is a default change plus a note in the script docs.
3. **A CI check that the two corpora agree** on ingredient name → term.id for every shared
   name. That is the assertion #266 verified by hand; making it a test would have caught
   #257's gap the day it landed.

(3) is the one that turns this from "remember to do it" into something mechanical, and it
is cheap — the check above runs in well under a minute.
title: Corpus fixes reach data/normalized_yaml but not its derived twin data/merge_yaml/merged

body:
Found while investigating whether CultureMech could resolve its own ingredient name variants, as an alternative to consuming MIM's label index (#260).

**It cannot, and the reason is data rather than schema.**

## The schema supports synonyms

`src/culturemech/schema/culturemech.yaml` defines `IngredientDescriptor.synonyms`, an `IngredientSynonym` class with `synonym_text` / `synonym_type`, and `MediaRecipe.synonyms`. The modelling is there and is fine.

## The data does not

Measured across `data/normalized_yaml/**` (15,407 media files):

| | count |
|---|---|
| ingredient entries | 169,573 |
| — carrying any synonym | **3,130 (1.8%)** |
| distinct ingredient names | 3,928 |
| — that *ever* carry a synonym | **11 (0.3%)** |
| **distinct synonym strings in the entire corpus** | **22** |

The 22 are a handful of hardcoded pairs repeated across thousands of media:

    NaCl (783)  ·  table salt (783)  ·  casein peptone (626)
    dextrose (621)  ·  D-glucose (621)  ·  tryptone (464)

So eleven ingredients have synonyms and 3,917 do not. For comparison, MIM publishes **5,656 synonyms** over 2,841 preferred terms in `docs/data/label_index.csv`.

## Why it matters

Ingredient names in this corpus vary heavily in surface form — `MgSO4·7H2O` / `MgSO4 x 7 H2O` / `magnesium sulfate heptahydrate`, `Glucose` / `D-Glucose` / `Dextrose`, `KOH` / `Potassium hydroxide`. Without synonyms, each variant is a separate unjoinable string, which is why:

- the same substance appears many times under different names with independently-assigned `term.id` values that then disagree (68 such disagreements measured against MIM in #260)
- half of CultureMech's names cannot be resolved from MIM's SSSOM either, because SSSOM also publishes only preferred terms — the join has to go through a synonym-bearing index

## Two ways forward, not exclusive

**1. Consume MIM's `label_index.csv` (#260).** It already carries the 5,656 synonyms and resolves 2,215 of CultureMech's 3,928 names. This is the cheap path and needs no data entry here.

**2. Populate `synonyms` from that same index**, so CultureMech records become self-describing rather than depending on a join at read time. This is the more durable path but is a bulk data change.

Worth noting the 22 existing strings look hand-seeded rather than derived — `table salt` for NaCl is not a media-recipe usage — so whatever populated them was not a systematic pass and there is no existing pipeline to extend.

## Not urgent on its own

Nothing is *broken* by the absence; it is a missing capability that makes the divergence in #260 hard to avoid. Filing so the 1.8%/0.3% figures are on record rather than rediscovered.
title: Ingredient synonyms are modelled but effectively unpopulated — 22 distinct strings corpus-wide

body:
Found reviewing #261, and contradicted by that PR's own data.

`scripts/identify_cocktail_stocks.py` emits a `volume_is_invariant` column alongside a
modal volume and an observation count. Its current output:

| stock | records | obs n | modal | invariant |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Trace element solution (Vishniac & Santer) | 8 | **2** | 5 ml 100% | **yes** |
| Trace Metals (500x) | 6 | **2** | 2 ml 100% | **yes** |
| Standard vitamin solution | 7 | 3 | 10 ml 100% | **yes** |
| Vitamin solution CA | 1 | **1** | 1 ml 100% | **yes** |

`invariant: yes` on n=1 and n=2 is not a finding, it is a restatement of the sample size.

#261 then read the actual media and found the Vishniac row is **false**: MediaDive medium
142 adds that stock at **0.2 ml** while medium 69 adds it at **5 ml** — a 25× spread the
n=2 sample missed entirely. Six records in #261 correctly received 0.2 ml candidates,
against a column claiming the stock is invariant at 5 ml.

This matters because the column reads as license to generalize a volume across media,
which is exactly the shortcut PR #251 established does not hold and which this script's
own docstring warns against. A curator skimming the report gets the opposite message from
the table than from the prose.

Suggested: require a minimum n (5? 10?) before `invariant` can be `yes`, and emit
`insufficient-sample` rather than `yes`/`no` below it. Also worth reporting the observed
range, not just the mode — `0.2–5 ml` would have made the Vishniac case obvious.
title: identify_cocktail_stocks reports a volume as 'invariant' on samples as small as n=2

body:
Found reviewing #261, which fixed the cause but not the existing records.

`apply_cocktail_nesting.split_parts` used `dict()` to copy an ingredient being split
across two stocks. That is a **shallow** copy, so the nested `term` and
`mediaingredientmech_chebi_term` dicts stayed shared with the source ingredient — and the
two copies land in *different* `solutions:` entries. `yaml.dump` serializes a shared
object as an anchor plus an alias:

```yaml
  - preferred_term: Nicotinic acid
    term: &id001
      id: CHEBI:15940
      label: Nicotinic acid
  ...
  - preferred_term: Nicotinic acid
    term: *id001
```

Why it matters beyond aesthetics: the two solutions alias **one object**. Any consumer
that loads the record and edits one solution's `term.label` silently edits the other's.
It also makes review harder — a reviewer cannot see the aliased value at the alias site.

#261 switched to `copy.deepcopy`, so no new records get anchors (verified: the count
stayed at 34 across a 94-record apply). The 34 written earlier still have them:

```
$ grep -rl "&id00" data/normalized_yaml | wc -l
34
```

Fix is a load-with-alias-expansion and re-dump over those 34. Worth confirming while
doing it that the aliased values really are identical in each case, rather than assuming
the alias was harmless.
title: 34 records carry YAML anchors/aliases from the pre-deepcopy split path

body:
Found reviewing #261.

#261 resolves KOMODO-sourced cocktails through their base medium number and classifies
41 records as `CROSS_MEDIUM_INFERENCE` because the fetched medium's name disagrees with
the record's. That class currently mixes two very different situations:

**Genuine upstream rename** — the medium is right, the name moved:
`komodo.medium:69` is `THIOBACILLUS NOVELLUS medium` here and `STARKEYA NOVELLA MEDIUM`
in MediaDive. Same organism; *Thiobacillus novellus* was reclassified as *Starkeya
novella*. The volume could legitimately be asserted.

**Genuine #244 collision** — the medium number means different things on each side:
`komodo.medium:294` is `PELOBACTER ACIDIGALLICI MEDIUM` here and `SYNTROPHUS HQGö1
MEDIUM` upstream. Different medium. The proposed volume is probably **wrong**, not merely
unverified, and the candidate should be withdrawn rather than left for someone to promote.

#261 treats both conservatively (candidate, never assertion, counterevidence naming both
media), which is safe but leaves the wrong ones sitting in the corpus looking like open
proposals.

Triage needs a taxonomy check rather than string similarity.
`scripts/audit_mediadive_ids.py` already carries `KNOWN_UPSTREAM_RENAMES`, and
`src/culturemech/taxonomy/similarity.py` exists — between them a rename should be
distinguishable from a collision.

Proposed outcomes:
- rename confirmed → promote to `READ_FROM_THIS_MEDIUM`
- collision confirmed → delete the candidate and report the record as unresolvable
- neither → leave as-is

Note the nesting itself is not in question in either case: every moved row matched the
stock composition on name AND value, so those rows are flattened stock entries regardless
of which medium supplied the volume. Only the volume is at stake.
title: Triage the 41 KOMODO candidates whose medium name disagrees: renames vs #244 collisions

body:
Filed from the MediaIngredientMech side, where MediaIngredientMech#138 has been fixing CultureMech/MIM grounding divergences one row at a time since it was opened. The divergences are systemic, and there is a published artifact that retires the class.

## The measurement

Joining CultureMech's 3,916 distinct ingredient names against MIM:

| | count |
|---|---|
| names with a CultureMech `term.id` | 1,584 |
| names MIM can resolve | 2,112 |
| both have an opinion | 1,569 |
| — agree | 1,501 |
| — **disagree** | **68** (3,386 occurrences) |
| CultureMech has a term, MIM does not | 59 |
| **MIM resolves, CultureMech has no term** | **543** |

So MIM already resolves *more* of CultureMech's own ingredient names than CultureMech does (2,112 vs 1,584).

## The 68 disagreements favour MIM everywhere I checked

| ingredient | occ | CultureMech | MIM | which is right |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `EDTA` | 520 | `CHEBI:64755` EDTA(2−) | `CHEBI:4735` free acid | MIM — ChEBI defines the (2−) as deprotonation of *two of four* carboxy groups; the label asserts no charge |
| `4-Aminobenzoic acid` | 141 | `CHEBI:194474` **4-ammoniobenzoate** | `CHEBI:30753` the acid | MIM — a zwitterion; CAS `150-13-0` and 1,968 MIM occurrences say the neutral acid |
| `Ca-pantothenate` | 137 | `CHEBI:29032` bare anion | `CHEBI:31345` calcium salt | MIM |
| `Beef heart` | 164 | `UBERON:0000948` (the organ) | `FOODON:00004410` | MIM — a food product, not an anatomical structure |
| `Calf brains` | 164 | `UBERON:0000955` (the organ) | `UNMAPPED_0170` | MIM — honestly unmapped |
| `Infusion from Potatoes` | 1 | `FOODON:03316428` **sweets** | `UNMAPPED_0251` | MIM — and CultureMech stores `label: 'potato extract'` against that id, which FOODON calls `sweets` |

Note the last two rows are exactly MediaIngredientMech#138's remaining items, and `4-Aminobenzoic acid` alone is **251 entries** across 251 files here, every one a PABA label with an empty `term.label`.

## The proposal

Consume **`MediaIngredientMech/docs/data/label_index.csv`** as the resolution source, and keep local `term.id` only as a fallback.

    label,match_type,identifier,preferred_term,ontology_id,mapping_status

8,492 rows — 2,841 preferred_terms + 5,651 synonyms — regenerated on every MIM export and gated in MIM's CI. Join on the normalised `label`; take `identifier`. It covers **2,215** of CultureMech's 3,916 names today, against 1,584 grounded locally.

`mapping_status` matters: `REJECTED` means the label resolves but its MIM record is a merge tombstone, and `identifier` already points at the merge target. Do **not** filter those out — follow the identifier. (Dropping them is what made `Glucose`, 2,120 occurrences, publish as REJECTED in culturebotai-claw#67.)

## What CultureMech would need to accept

- **59 names lose their local grounding**, of which a few are genuinely absent from MIM — notably `Peptic digest of soybean meal` (464 occ, `FOODON:03315720`) and `DL-Tyrosine` (18). These should be contributed to MIM as records rather than dropped. Most of the rest are ontology-label matches that MediaIngredientMech#365 proposes to index, which would close them automatically.
- **Two MIM-side prerequisites**, both tracked in MediaIngredientMech#365: index `ontology_label` as a third `match_type`, and fix MediaIngredientMech#360 (merge tombstones still advertise an `ontology_id` they no longer assert, which mis-routes `D-Glucose`, 589 occ).

## Why not just fix the 251 rows

That is what MediaIngredientMech#138 has been doing, and the divergence reappears with every curation pass on either side — MIM has merged, regrounded or re-graded several hundred records in the last month alone, and none of it reaches CultureMech. A one-time correction fixes 251 rows; consuming the index fixes the mechanism.

Companion issue: MediaIngredientMech#365.
title: Resolve ingredient groundings from MIM's published label index instead of local term.id

body:
Found reviewing #257; noted in passing in #256, filed separately because it is a
distinct and mechanically-checkable class.

`term.label` is expected to be the ontology term's label. In much of the corpus it is
the ingredient string from the source recipe instead:

| id | label as stored | rows | actual CHEBI label |
|---|---|---:|---|
| CHEBI:31795 | `MgSO4 x 7 H2O` | 6,150 | magnesium sulfate heptahydrate |
| CHEBI:31795 | `Magnesium sulphate heptahydrate` | 1 | (spelling variant) |
| CHEBI:31795 | `` (empty) | 49 | — |
| CHEBI:17439 | `Cyanocobalamin` | 23 | cyanocob(III)alamin |

The same id therefore appears under many different labels, and both forms coexist for
the same term (CHEBI:17439 carries its real label in 156 rows and the ingredient string
in 23).

Consequences:
- Label-based review and diffing is defeated — a reviewer cannot eyeball whether an id
  is right, which is exactly the check that would have caught the wrong-compound
  groundings fixed in #257.
- Empty labels (49 on CHEBI:31795 alone) carry no signal at all.

The ingredient string is already preserved in `preferred_term`, so `term.label` can be
refilled from the ontology without losing anything. Suggested: a checked artifact that
refills `term.label` from CHEBI and fails CI when an id and its label disagree.
title: term.label often carries the ingredient string instead of the ontology label

body:
Found reviewing #257. Pre-existing — #257 did not create it (Dextrose sat on three
distinct ids before that PR and three after) — but the review made it visible.

`Dextrose` is grounded three different ways in the corpus today:

| name | id | label | rows |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Dextrose | CHEBI:17234 | glucose | 157 |
| Dextrose | CHEBI:4167 | D-glucopyranose | 74 |
| Dextrose | CHEBI:17634 | D-glucose | 27 |

Dextrose is, by definition, D-glucose, so CHEBI:17634 is the defensible target and the
other 231 rows should move. `alpha-D-Glucose` (CHEBI:17925) and `beta-D-Glucose`
(ungrounded, 16 rows) are genuinely distinct anomers and should stay distinct.

Also ungrounded in the family: `beta-D-Glucose` (16), `D--Glucose` (6, and that double
hyphen looks like a normalization artifact worth chasing separately),
`Dextrose (BD 215530)` (3), `α-D-Glucose monohydrate` (2).

This matters more than tidiness: `culturemech_term_id` outranks `mim_id` downstream
(#256), so each variant propagates as a different compound into kg-microbe, and a
consumer counting glucose-containing media gets the wrong answer.

Worth checking whether the same split affects other high-frequency ingredients before
fixing glucose specifically — the fix should be a general consistency check, not a
one-compound patch.
title: One ingredient name, several CHEBI ids: the glucose family is split four ways

body:
Reported downstream as MediaIngredientMech#138 (kg-microbe loader precedence). The
investigation confirms the reporter's framing: **the hazard originates in CultureMech,
and no MIM-side fix can reach it.**

## Why a MIM fix can't reach it

kg-microbe's loader resolves an ingredient with
`best_primary([chebi_id, culturemech_term_id, mim_id, kg_microbe_node_id, cas_rn])`.
`culturemech_term_id` outranks `mim_id`, and `culturemech_term_id` is populated from
**our** `term.id`. So when MIM corrects `mim_id`, the consumer still picks our value.
MIM can only fix rows we don't have an opinion on.

## Our MIM "link" carries no MIM opinion

`mediaingredientmech_chebi_term` is effectively a self-link:

| `mediaingredientmech_chebi_term.id` vs our own `term.id` | rows |
|---|---:|
| identical | 119,577 |
| different | 554 |

That is by design — `scripts/migrate_legacy_mim_to_chebi.py` states it uses "the
ingredient's OWN CHEBI id and label" and deliberately does not import MIM's
`preferred_term`. The consequence was not intended: the field looks like corroboration
from MIM but is our own assertion echoed back, so it can never carry a correction.

1,682 legacy `mediaingredientmech_term` (`MediaIngredientMech:NNNNNN`) links also remain
across 1,506 records, pointing at a scheme MIM has retired.

## Are we consuming MIM's SSSOM? Essentially no

MIM publishes `mappings/ingredient_mappings.sssom.tsv`. Exactly one script reads it —
`scripts/audit_missing_roles.py` — and only to report role-coverage gaps. **No grounding
path consumes it.** We generate our own (`output/culturemech_chebi_mappings.sssom.tsv`)
and ground independently.

## Blast radius: 6,680 ingredient rows, 115 distinct names

Where both sides have an opinion on the same ingredient name and disagree, our value wins
downstream. It is **not** simply "MIM is right" — it runs both ways, which is why this
needs curation rather than a bulk overwrite:

| name | ours | MIM | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| magnesium sulfate heptahydrate (160) | CHEBI:86463 **potassium aluminium sulfate** | CHEBI:31795 magnesium sulfate heptahydrate | **ours is the wrong compound** |
| glucose (522) | CHEBI:42758 **aldehydo-D-glucose** | CHEBI:17234 glucose | ours is the open-chain form |
| d-glucose (138) | CHEBI:42758 **aldehydo-D-glucose** | CHEBI:17634 D-glucose | ours is the open-chain form |
| 4-aminobenzoic acid (135) | CHEBI:194474 4-ammoniobenzoate | CHEBI:30753 4-aminobenzoic acid | MIM better (neutral acid) |
| edta (520) | CHEBI:64755 EDTA(2-) | CHEBI:4735 ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid | MIM better (reagent as supplied) |
| mgso4·7h2o (407) | CHEBI:31795 magnesium sulfate heptahydrate | CHEBI:32599 magnesium sulfate | **ours better** |
| vitamin b12 (2004) | CHEBI:17439 cyanocob(III)alamin | CHEBI:176843 vitamin B12 | ours more specific; defensible |
| thiamine (134) | CHEBI:26948 vitamin B1 | CHEBI:18385 thiamine(1+) | both imperfect |

Note we are also internally inconsistent: `mgso4·7h2o` → CHEBI:31795 but
`magnesium sulfate heptahydrate` → CHEBI:86463, two names for one substance.

## The Cobalamine row specifically

| our ingredient | our `term.id` | is | rows |
|---|---|---|---:|
| `Cobalamine` | CHEBI:30411 | cobalamin | 2 |
| `Cobalamine` | CHEBI:28911 | cob(III)alamin | 1 |
| `Cobalamin` | CHEBI:28911 | cob(III)alamin | 3 |
| `cobalamin` | CHEBI:28911 | cob(III)alamin | 1 |

MIM#138's table describes CHEBI:28911 as "Cobalamine"; it is actually `cob(III)alamin`.
The correct target depends on MediaIngredientMech#363 (open: should `Cobalamine` be
cyanocobalamin, CHEBI:17439, as media practice implies?). **No corpus change here until
that resolves** — 7 rows, low urgency, and guessing is how the current state arose.

## Also: id↔label drift

Some rows carry the ingredient string in `term.label` instead of the ontology label
(e.g. CHEBI:17439 labelled "Cyanocobalamin" in 23 rows, "cyanocob(III)alamin" — the real
label — in 156). Independent of the above but it defeats label-based review.

## Proposed work

1. Fix the outright-wrong compounds (magnesium sulfate heptahydrate; glucose/d-glucose)
   and the internal mgso4 inconsistency. — highest value, unambiguous
2. Consume MIM's SSSOM as a **divergence check** in CI so new disagreements surface at
   review time instead of downstream.
3. Stop presenting `mediaingredientmech_chebi_term` as corroboration, or populate it from
   MIM so it means what its name implies.
4. Reground/retire the 1,682 legacy `MediaIngredientMech:NNNNNN` links.
5. Curate the remaining divergences name by name; report the agreed set back to MIM.
title: Our groundings override MIM downstream: 6,680 divergent rows, some outright wrong compounds (MIM#138)

body:
Found reviewing MediaIngredientMech PR #302 (closes MIM #210).

`conf/id_label_targets.yaml:93` here sets:

```yaml
max_accession:
  CHEBI: 300000
```

That is an order of magnitude below every sibling prefix and **below ChEBI's own accession range**. Measured against the shared local semsql build:

```
max CHEBI accession in build: 747618   (release 252)
CHEBI:747127 -> gepotidacin
```

So the ceiling does not describe CHEBI's accession space. Any ChEBI term newer than the local build that fails to resolve is reported `ID_OUT_OF_RANGE`, whose documented meaning in `validate_id_label_correspondence.py:142` is *"a foreign identifier (typically a PubChem CID) wearing an OBO prefix"*.

That wording is not hypothetical harm. In MIM it produced #193: 17 real ChEBI terms demoted to UNMAPPED on the strength of the verdict, 11 of which resolved locally the whole time (MIM #197, #205).

## Scope here

`scripts/validate_id_label_correspondence.py` is byte-identical between the two repos (`md5 312ee4af1351c54bcce065829ac0083b`), so the *logic* is shared. `conf/id_label_targets.yaml` is **not** shared (different hashes), which is why fixing MIM did not fix this.

I have not measured CultureMech's exposure — someone should check whether any CURIE in this corpus currently lands on the ceiling before deciding urgency. In MIM the count was 0 at fix time, making it preventive rather than corrective.

## Fix

Raise `CHEBI` to `1000000`, matching what MIM shipped and what `MediaIngredientMech/src/mediaingredientmech/curie.py::MAX_ACCESSION` already used. The rationale to record with it: the ceiling tracks **the digit count of the foreign namespace it separates out** (PubChem CIDs reach 8 digits), not a guess at how far ChEBI has minted — so it moves when PubChem changes width, not when ChEBI mints higher.

Nothing that fails today starts passing: the ceiling is consulted only for ids that already failed to resolve, and `ID_NOT_FOUND` and `ID_OUT_OF_RANGE` are both in `_ERROR_VERDICTS`. It changes which of two fatal diagnoses a curator is shown.

Related: MediaIngredientMech #210, #197, #205, #193.
title: conf/id_label_targets.yaml carries the same wrong CHEBI ceiling (300000) that MIM just fixed

body:
Found while extending the #150 cocktail repair to KOMODO-sourced records.

To reach a record's stock composition, its medium id is resolved to MediaDive
(`mediadive.medium:<n>` directly, or `komodo.medium:<n>` via the tracked
`komodo_dsmz_mappings.json`). Fetching that medium and comparing NAMES shows the id
frequently points at an unrelated medium:

```
KOMODO 1010  "Artificial SEAWATER MEDIUM"    -> MediaDive 1010 "DESULFOPILA CORRODENS MEDIUM"
KOMODO 294   "PELOBACTER ACIDIGALLICI MEDIUM"-> MediaDive 294  "SYNTROPHUS HQGo1 MEDIUM"
KOMODO 903   "THERMOANAEROBACTERIUM medium"  -> MediaDive 903  "CALDANAEROBIUS MEDIUM"
mediadive.medium:508  "PYRODICTIUM ABYSSI medium" -> MediaDive 508 "CARBOXYDOTHERMUS MEDIUM (HETEROTROPH)"
```

**165 of 312** resolved cocktail records disagreed by name. Note the last example
carries a **direct** `mediadive.medium:` id — so this is not only a KOMODO-mapping
artifact; some corpus MediaDive ids are themselves wrong or stale.

## Why it matters
Any tool that pulls upstream data keyed on these ids (composition backfill, stock
volumes, cross-references, KG edges) will silently import another medium's data.
The #150 applier guards against it by comparing names before use — that guard is
what surfaced this — but the underlying ids remain wrong in the corpus.

## Likely causes, not yet separated
- MediaDive renumbering since the KOMODO/MediaDive snapshots were taken.
- KOMODO's own `dsmz_medium_number` being an identity default (43.5% of that mapping
  is `komodo_id == dsmz_medium_number`) rather than a verified cross-reference.
- Genuine mis-assignment during import.

## Suggested work
1. Audit all `mediadive.medium:` / `komodo.medium:` ids in the corpus against the
   live MediaDive `/rest/media` name list, not just the cocktail subset.
2. Where the name disagrees, either re-resolve to the correct id (by name, with the
   collision caveat from #239) or mark the id unverified.
3. Consider recording a `verified_against` datestamp so a future renumbering is
   detectable rather than silent.

One known instance already in the corpus: `sulfurospirillum_alkalitolerans_medium`
carries `mediadive.medium:1298`, which is "SULFUROSPIRILLUM TAMANENSIS MEDIUM"; no
*S. alkalitolerans* medium exists in MediaDive at all. Its #243 nesting is still
substantively correct (the moved components matched standard DSMZ stocks by name AND
value), but the id it cites is wrong.
title: Corpus media_term ids disagree with MediaDive: 165 cocktail records resolve to a different medium

body:
Scoped successor to the composition-backfill residual of #175. Splitting it out
because it is an **id-resolution + API-backfill** task, not the flagging/cleanup
#175 covered (which is done).

## The finding (verified against the live MediaDive API)
225 media have no usable composition and are flagged `incomplete_composition`
(#234). They are **not uniformly empty at source** — the emptiness is largely a
broken id mapping in CultureMech's import:

- `KOMODO_3136_Fastidious_Anaerobe_Agar` is empty, carrying `komodo.medium:3136`
  ("DSMZ Medium: 3136" in its notes is the KOMODO/ModelSEED id). The real medium is
  **MediaDive 1203**, which HAS composition (`/rest/medium-composition/1203` →
  horse blood + agar base + deionized water). Wrong id → no composition pulled.

So the composition often exists upstream; CultureMech just isn't pointing at it.

## Why it's not a trivial refill
- The empty records carry **KOMODO / JCM ids**, not MediaDive composition ids — no
  direct handle to re-fetch from.
- **Name-matching is unsafe**: JCM `J806 "GS MEDIUM"` collides with DSMZ
  `1397 "GS MEDIUM"` (37 components) — matching by name can import a *different*
  recipe under a shared name.
- **JCM-sourced media (`J*`) 404 on MediaDive's composition endpoint** — MediaDive
  catalogues them (source: JCM, link to jcm.riken.jp GRMD) but stores no
  composition; those need the **JCM GRMD** source instead (cf. the `scrape-jcm-media`
  skill), not MediaDive.
- Some DSMZ numeric ids (44, 77, 1591, 1850) also 404 — genuine per-medium gaps.

## Rough coverage (quick pass, needs firming up)
Of 225 empty media: ~73 name-match a MediaDive entry; only ~6 resolve to a numeric
MediaDive id; of those only a couple confidently share the medium (e.g. 1203). So
reliable recovery is blocked on **correct per-record id resolution**, not data
availability.

## Proposed work
1. Resolve each empty KOMODO/JCM record to its correct upstream id — MediaDive
   numeric id for DSMZ media, JCM GRMD id for `J*` media — using a safer signal than
   name alone (source + strain/organism cross-refs, the DSMZ PDF link, the JCM GRMD
   link already in the record).
2. Pull composition from the right API (MediaDive `/rest/medium-composition/{id}`;
   JCM GRMD for `J*`), map to the CultureMech ingredient/concentration schema, apply
   with a curation event, clearing the `incomplete_composition` flag on success.
3. Leave genuinely source-absent media flagged.

## Sources / snapshots
- MediaDive live REST API (`/rest/media`, `/rest/medium-composition/{id}`), checked
  today.
- kg-microbe mediadive transform `data/transformed/mediadive` (kgm snapshot
  2026-08-05) has composition for 3,081/3,327 media as `medium -> solution -> CHEBI`,
  but the specific empty media resolve to 0 there too (same id/coverage issue).

Successor to #175.
title: Resolve KOMODO/JCM media to their real MediaDive/JCM ids and backfill composition

body:
Found while retiring test_medium_123 (#175, PR #237): regenerating the recipe/source
indexes produced a large diff that was NOT about the deletion — it added
`organism_culture_type` to many per-record entries, drift that had accumulated
since #142/#223 (which backfilled that slot) without the indexes being regenerated.

## Why CI didn't catch it
`tests/test_recipe_indexes.py` guards the record **set**, not per-record content:
- `test_index_count_matches_directory` — counts
- `test_index_entry_count_matches_count_field` — counts
- `test_index_filenames_all_exist` / `test_every_yaml_in_the_directory_is_indexed` — paths/coverage

None compares a per-record entry to a fresh render of that record. So a corpus PR
that changes a *field* the index embeds (organism_culture_type, medium_type,
composition_type, …) leaves the indexes stale and every index test still passes.

## This is the #145 class again
A tracked derived artifact drifting silently from its source with no guard. The
indexes ARE freshness-guarded for the failure mode #125 cared about (a moved/renamed
record → stale path), but not for field-level content drift.

## Suggested fix
Add a freshness check that regenerates each index to a temp path and byte-compares
(normalizing the `generated` timestamp), the same shape used by the
derived-artifacts harness (#203) and the merge_yaml freshness audit (#217). That
would have failed on the organism_culture_type drift. Alternatively, register the
indexes in the derived-artifacts CHECKABLE set.

Low urgency (the indexes are consumed by the browser/pages, and #237 just
regenerated them current), but it is a real hole in a guard that exists precisely
to prevent index drift.
title: Recipe-index freshness guard misses field-level drift (only checks record set/counts/paths)

body:
Found while repairing the media half of #175 (PR for the 100 placeholder-only
media).

The placeholder ingredient "See source for composition" (value `variable`) is not
confined to media: **~4,775 stock-solution records** carry it too. They were
deliberately excluded from the #175 media repair (`is_solution_record`), because:

- #175 is scoped to media composition (11,094 media, 4.2% empty).
- A solution's "composition" behaves differently from a medium's, so the same
  repair shape (empty + `incomplete_composition`) may or may not be right for a
  stock solution — that needs its own look.

The `curate_placeholder_composition.py` script added in the #175 PR already detects
these if its `is_solution_record` guard is dropped, so the mechanical repair is
available; what's missing is the decision on whether solutions with no imported
composition should be emptied-and-flagged the same way, or handled differently
(e.g. many may be resolvable via their `mediadive.solution:*` id).
title: ~4,775 stock-solution records carry the 'See source for composition' placeholder (#175 spin-off)

body:
From resolving #168 (PR for the content manifest).

#168 grouped two tracked review manifests. They turned out to need different
treatment:

- `media_content_review_manifest.tsv` — reproducible from the tracked corpus,
  consumed by `propose_media_variant_links`, was ~10k lines stale. Refreshed and
  freshness-guarded in the #168 PR. Its no-reader siblings (json / groups / summary)
  were untracked (#157/#167 pattern).

- **`media_growth_review_manifest.{tsv,json,md}`** is the problem this issue tracks.
  Its writer `build_media_growth_review_manifest.py` reads
  `workspace/reports/growth_evidence_proposals[_backfill]`, and **`workspace/` is
  gitignored** — 0 tracked files under those proposal dirs. So the manifest is a
  snapshot of one machine's local proposal state, NOT reproducible from tracked
  data. This is the #121 anti-pattern (a tracked artifact derived from gitignored
  inputs).

It is consumed — `build_media_growth_review_html.py` reads it to render HTML — so
it is not simply category-3 untrackable. The options:

1. **Track its inputs.** Move the growth-evidence proposals out of `workspace/` into
   a tracked path, making the manifest reproducible and freshness-checkable like the
   content one. Correct if those proposals are curation products worth keeping.
2. **Untrack the manifest** (and its HTML consumer's tracked output, if any). Correct
   if the proposals are genuinely machine-local scratch.

This is a maintainer call about what the growth-evidence proposals *are*, which is
why it is filed rather than resolved in the #168 PR. Until then the growth manifest
cannot be given the same guard the content manifest now has.
title: media_growth_review_manifest is derived from gitignored workspace/ — not reproducibly checkable (#168 follow-up)

body:
From review of #214.

`tests/test_concentration_plausibility.py::test_the_gate_baselines_match_the_current_corpus`
guards the **row** baseline against becoming vacuous:

```python
assert rows_baseline - len(rows) <= 200, (
    f"gate baseline {rows_baseline} is {rows_baseline - len(rows)} above the "
    "actual count — tighten it or it will never fire")
```

but the **cocktail** baseline — which #214 itself calls "the sharper of the two"
— gets only:

```python
assert COCKTAIL_BASELINE > 0
```

So as the 579-record cocktail backlog is repaired under #150, `COCKTAIL_BASELINE`
can drift far above the real count and the sharper gate silently stops being able
to fire, with no test noticing. The row baseline's ≤200 check partially masks this
(repairing cocktails also drops rows), but that is incidental, not a guarantee.

## Fix
Add a symmetric anti-vacuous assertion for the cocktail baseline: compute the
current flattened-cocktail count and assert `COCKTAIL_BASELINE - actual <= tol`.
Requires counting cocktails from parsed records in the test (the script does it as
`sum(1 for s in summary if s["flattened_cocktail"] == "yes")`).

Low severity: current baseline (579) equals the actual count, so nothing is vacuous
today. Filed rather than folded into #214 because it hardens the gate's self-test
rather than fixing a defect in what #214 ships.
title: Cocktail baseline lacks the anti-vacuous check the row baseline has (#214 review)

body:
Found reviewing the downstream sync of #216 (`CultureBotAI/MediaIngredientMech#262`).

`scripts/chem_formula.py` declares an explicit public API:

```python
__all__ = [
    "looks_like_formula",
    "parse_formula",
    "parse_ontology_formula",
    "compare_formulas",
    "build_formula_lookup",
]
```

#216 added `hydration_states` — a documented public helper, called from `validate_id_label_correspondence.py` and covered by its own tests — but did not add it to `__all__`. (`_label_water_units` is private and correctly omitted.)

**Impact is cosmetic:** every real caller uses `chem_formula.hydration_states(...)` on the module object, which works regardless of `__all__`. It only bites `from chem_formula import *`, and can make linters treat the name as non-public.

Worth folding into the next hub change that touches this file rather than spending a dedicated hub PR + spoke re-sync round trip on it, since each vendored change costs a `.vendored_canon_ref` bump in every spoke.
title: chem_formula.hydration_states is missing from __all__

body:
Surfaced while building the merge_yaml freshness audit (#215, PR #217).

`data/merge_yaml/` tracks **two** merged corpora:

| dir | tracked files | written by | read by |
|---|--:|---|---|
| `merged/` | 6,104 | `just merge-recipes` (default `--output-dir`) | `verify-merges` |
| `merged_2026/` | 4,291 | (unknown recipe) | `gen-media-pages` / `generate-pages.yaml`, `recipe_index.json` |

The counts differ, so they are genuinely different generations, not copies. The
freshness audit in #217 checks `merged/`. But the corpus that actually gets
**rendered and published** is `merged_2026/`, and it is even further from a fresh
run (4,291 vs 6,104 vs 4,595-fresh).

`--tracked-dir merged_2026` is **not** a valid workaround: the audit regenerates
with the default fingerprinter, and `merged_2026/` may have been produced with the
`HierarchyAwareFingerprinter` (or other parameters), so the diff would conflate
generation parameters with drift.

## The questions to settle
1. Which corpus is canonical — `merged/` or `merged_2026/`?
2. How was `merged_2026/` generated (which recipe / fingerprinter / when)? No
   justfile recipe writes to it that I can find.
3. Once (1)/(2) are answered, the freshness audit should target the canonical,
   consumed corpus rather than `merged/`.

This is part of the policy half of #215 (what is `merge_yaml` for), but the
published-corpus-is-ungated angle is concrete and worth its own tracking.
title: Two divergent tracked merge_yaml corpora (merged/ vs merged_2026/); the published one has no freshness check

body:
Surfaced while building the merge_yaml freshness audit (#215, PR #217).

`merge_recipes` fingerprints normalized_yaml into **6,286 unique recipe groups**,
but a fresh run writes only **4,595 files** to `merge_yaml/merged/`. The ~1,691
missing records are lost to filename collisions:

```python
# src/culturemech/merge/merge_recipes.py (write loop)
filename = merged_recipe['name'].replace('/', '_').replace(' ', '_') + '.yaml'
output_path = args.output_dir / filename
...
with open(output_path, 'w', ...):   # later group with same filename overwrites earlier
```

Two distinct groups whose canonical names collapse to the same filename (after the
`/`→`_` and ` `→`_` substitutions) overwrite each other silently. The last writer
wins; the earlier group's record is gone with no warning.

## Why it matters
- It is **silent data loss**: 27% of the groups the merge identifies never reach
  disk. `merge_stats.json` reports 6,286 output recipes, but only 4,595 exist.
- Which group survives depends on `groups.items()` iteration order, so the loss is
  reproducible but opaque.

## Suggested fix
Detect collisions and either (a) disambiguate the filename (append a short
fingerprint suffix), or (b) fail loudly with the colliding names. At minimum,
count collisions and report them in `merge_stats.json` so the group-vs-file gap
is visible.

## Related
The freshness audit added in #217 compares tracked vs fresh **file sets**, so it
already reflects the post-collision reality — but this drop is a defect in the
merge itself, independent of the drift #215 tracks.
title: merge_recipes silently drops ~1,691 records to filename collisions (6,286 groups → 4,595 files)

body:
From review of #214.

`data/merge_yaml/merged*/` holds **10,433 tracked YAML media records** — real
records with CultureMech ids, not summaries:

```
data/merge_yaml/merged/.../TYL_medium.yaml
  id: CultureMech:008339
  name: TYL medium
  category: bacterial
```

Every corpus gate in this repo scans `data/normalized_yaml/**` only. Running the
plausibility detectors over a 4,000-record sample of `merge_yaml`:

```
5,005 implausible concentration rows
```

So the defect #150 exists to gate is present there too, in tracked files, with no
check on it.

## This is wider than one gate

`chebi-consistency.yaml` documents the same limitation and reasons it away:

> The derived `data/merge_yaml/**` files are NOT validated here, on the assumption
> that merge_yaml is always regenerated from normalized_yaml — an inconsistency
> introduced *only* in merge_yaml would not be caught by this gate. If merge_yaml
> ever becomes hand-edited, add it here.

I copied that caveat into the new workflow. It is accurate, but the assumption
behind it has never been tested, and the consequence is that **roughly half the
tracked media records in the repo are outside every quality gate**:

```
data/normalized_yaml   15,878 files   gated
data/merge_yaml        10,433 files   ungated
```

## The question to settle

Is `merge_yaml` genuinely derived, or has it drifted?

- If **derived**, a test should assert it can be regenerated from
  `normalized_yaml` — the same argument as #145's freshness checks. Nothing
  currently establishes that, so "it is derived" is an assumption, not a fact.
- If **drifted**, it is a second corpus and needs the same gates.
- If **obsolete**, it should not be tracked at all — 10,433 stale records are a
  liability, and untracking removes the failure mode rather than policing it
  (#157's third category).

Not addressed in #214, which gates what the detectors actually read. Filed because
"assumed derived, never verified" is precisely the shape that produced #121, #144,
#157 and #168.
title: Every corpus gate scans normalized_yaml only — 10,433 tracked records in merge_yaml are ungated

body:
From review of #212.

The budget collects `call` durations in a module-level dict in `tests/conftest.py`
and checks them in `pytest_sessionfinish`.

Under `pytest-xdist`, each worker has its own process and its own copy of that
dict. `pytest_sessionfinish` runs in the workers *and* on the controller, and the
controller's dict is **empty** — so the check would pass unconditionally while
appearing to run.

**Not currently possible:** xdist is neither in `pyproject.toml` nor importable in
the dev environment, and CI runs a plain `pytest`. Verified both.

**Why file it anyway:** the suite takes ~12 minutes locally and ~25–34 in CI, and
`-n auto` is the single most obvious response to that. Someone speeding up CI
would disable the guard as a side effect and get no signal — which is exactly the
class of silent failure #191 exists to prevent.

#212 makes the failure loud rather than silent: the check now refuses to report a
pass when it detects it is running under a worker, so adding xdist produces a
visible error instead of a quiet no-op.

**Real fix**, when xdist is actually wanted: send durations to the controller via
`pytest_xdist_make_report` / the `workeroutput` channel, and aggregate there.
Filed rather than implemented because building xdist support for a plugin nobody
runs is speculative — the loud failure is the honest interim.
title: The slow-test budget would silently stop working under pytest-xdist

body:
From review of #210.

`writes_artifact` binds names to the artifact path and then looks for writes
through those names. It has no scope analysis, so a local variable reusing a
module constant's name and writing somewhere else yields a false "yes":

```python
OUT = Path("data/report.tsv")

def unrelated():
    OUT = Path("/tmp/other.tsv")   # shadows the constant
    OUT.write_text("x")            # -> report.tsv reported as written
```

Measured behaviour on four adversarial cases:

```
shadowed name                 -> yes   (WRONG, should be no)
write to a different arg      -> no    correct
read here, write elsewhere    -> no    correct
mention only in a docstring   -> no    correct
```

**Not currently triggered.** I spot-checked ten artifacts with an established
writer and every claim held up. The one that looked wrong — `id_utils.py` writing
`culturemech_id_registry.tsv` — turned out to be correct: it binds the path as a
parameter default and writes it via `df.to_csv(output_path, ...)`. My verification
regex was the thing at fault, not the analyzer.

**Why it still matters.** #209 existed because a column asserted something it had
not established. A known false-positive mode in the replacement deserves to be
recorded rather than discovered later, especially since `writes` reads as the
stronger, more trustworthy column.

## Fix

Track scope — bind names per function rather than globally, and treat a local
assignment as shadowing. `ast` gives enough structure to do this without a full
dataflow pass. Alternatively, drop a binding when the same name is reassigned to
an expression that does NOT mention the basename.

Low priority while no real script triggers it, which is why it is filed rather
than fixed in #210.
title: artifact_writers can over-claim when a local variable shadows the path constant

body:
From #207's CI, where the #203 manifest guard fired correctly.

#207 adds `ID_REGISTRY = REPO_ROOT / "data" / "culturemech_id_registry.tsv"` to
`research_media.py`, which only **reads** the registry to build a resolution
index. `find_writers()` greps for the basename, so the manifest now records:

```
data/culturemech_id_registry.tsv
  writer: assign_culturemech_ids.py; refresh_id_registry.py;
          research_media.py; id_utils.py
```

`research_media.py` writes nothing. The column is named `writer` but holds
"scripts that mention this path".

**Impact is currently low.** Classification picks the first script matching the
generator prefixes (`refresh_id_registry.py`), so the *kind* stayed CURRENT_VIEW
and nothing downstream changed — only the evidence column got a wrong entry.

**Why it still matters.** That column is what a curator reads to decide whether an
artifact is a current view or a snapshot, and a reader listed as a writer is
misleading in exactly that judgement. It will also grow: every new consumer of a
tracked artifact adds itself.

## Fix options

1. Rename the column to `mentioned_by`, which is what it truthfully contains. No
   logic change, and honest.
2. Distinguish reads from writes by looking for the path near a write call
   (`write_text`, `open(..., "w")`, `DictWriter`) rather than anywhere in the file.
   More accurate, more fragile.
3. Both: keep `mentioned_by`, and add a `writes` column populated by (2) where it
   can be established.

(1) is the honest minimum and could ship immediately. The guard working as
designed is what surfaced this, which is the system behaving correctly.
title: derived_artifacts 'writer' column lists readers too — grep cannot tell them apart

body:
From review of #207.

`_media_files()` caches `sorted(MEDIA_DIR.glob("*/*.yaml"))` for the process. The
tier-1 and tier-2 index hits are guarded with `.exists()`, but the **fallback scan
is not** — it appends straight from the cached list:

```python
for path in _media_files():
    if _normal_key(path.stem) == normalized_target or ...:
        by_filename.append(path)      # no existence check
```

That was safe while the glob was re-run per call, since a deleted file simply
would not appear. With the list cached it does.

Reproduced:

```
warm the index, delete a record, resolve it by stem
  -> returns /.../bacterial/0_01_lb_seawater_medium.yaml   exists=False
```

The caller then does `load_media(path)`, which raises `FileNotFoundError` from
somewhere further away than the resolution that caused it.

**Who hits this:** any process that resolves, then moves or deletes records, then
resolves again — which is exactly the shape of a curation script. Recategorisations
like #114/#115/#120/#137/#143 move records in bulk.

## Also worth documenting: the opposite direction

A record CREATED after the cache warms is not found:

```
warm the index, create a record, resolve it by stem
  -> FileNotFoundError
```

That is inherent to caching and acceptable for a batch run, but it should be
stated rather than discovered. `reset_resolution_caches()` exists for callers that
mutate the corpus mid-process; nothing currently says so outside its docstring.

## Fix

Filter `path.exists()` in the scan tier as well, or have `_media_files()` drop
entries that have since disappeared. The first is cheaper and keeps the cost on
the rare path.
title: Cached media file list lets resolve_media_file return deleted paths

body:
From review of #205.

`record_io.write_record` guards its read-back comparison with `except OSError`:

```python
try:
    if path.read_text() == text:
        return False
except OSError:
    pass
path.write_text(text)
```

`UnicodeDecodeError` is a subclass of `ValueError`, **not** `OSError`, so it
escapes:

```
write_record(path_with_invalid_utf8, doc)
  -> UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xff in position 0
```

The intent of that `try` is clearly "if I cannot read the existing file, just
write" — and a file that is not valid UTF-8 is exactly that case.

**This is realistic, not theoretical.** Every corpus reader in this repo uses
`read_text(errors="replace")`, which exists because some records do not decode
cleanly. A curation script hitting one would crash partway through a batch rather
than repairing the file.

Fix: catch `(OSError, UnicodeDecodeError)`, or read bytes and compare against
`text.encode()`, which sidesteps decoding entirely and is closer to what the
comparison actually means.

## Lesser point, same function

`write_record` raises `FileNotFoundError` when the parent directory does not
exist. For corpus edits the directory always exists, so this is not urgent — but
`import_jcm_grmd.py` creates *new* records, and a writer used for creation is a
reasonable place to `mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` first.
title: write_record raises on a record with invalid UTF-8 instead of rewriting it

body:
From review of #203.

`find_writer()` greps for the artifact's basename and returns the **first** match.
`audit_derived_artifacts.py` lists all 7 checkable artifacts in its `CHECKABLE`
dict, so it matches every one of them — and for
`data/import_tracking/reports/unparsed_compositions.tsv` it sorts first:

```
unparsed_compositions.tsv -> writer: audit_derived_artifacts.py   (wrong)
                             actual: report_unparsed_compositions.py
```

The auditor's own existence changed the answer it reports. The `writer` column is
the *evidence* for each classification, so a circular attribution undermines the
manifest's purpose — and it will get worse as more artifacts are declared
checkable.

**Nine artifacts have multiple candidate writers**, and first-match wins:

```
data/culturemech_id_registry.tsv     3 candidates
  refresh_id_registry.py  assign_culturemech_ids.py  id_utils.py
reports/media_content_review_manifest.tsv   2 candidates
  propose_media_variant_links.py  build_media_content_review_manifest.py
```

For the registry the first happens to be correct — by alphabetical luck, not by
logic. For `media_content_review_manifest.tsv` the two writers are genuinely
different tools and picking one is arbitrary.

## Fix

1. Exclude `audit_derived_artifacts.py` from the writer search — a tool must not
   attribute artifacts to itself.
